Sanitary Fittings

Sanitary fittings are the cleanable stainless steel connections that hold a hygienic piping system together — the elbows, tees, reducers, ferrules, clamps, caps, and gaskets that route fluid without crevices, threads, or dead legs where bacteria or residue could collect. Cardinal Cooling Systems supplies a complete range of sanitary stainless steel fittings in 304 and 316L, polished to a 32Ra finish, manufactured to 3-A standards, and backed by mill test reports for full traceability.

What separates a sanitary fitting from an ordinary pipe fitting is the detail you can't see: a smooth, polished interior with no pockets or tight radii, so the whole line can be cleaned in place (CIP) or steamed without disassembly. That is why sanitary pipe fittings are the standard in data center liquid cooling, food and beverage, dairy, and pharmaceutical processing — anywhere fluid purity and cleanability are non-negotiable.

  • Bevel seat gaskets — sealing elements for bevel-seat and tri-clamp joints.
  • Hex nuts and clamp hardware — the union and clamp components that complete an assembly.

What makes a fitting “sanitary”

  • Crevice-free design. No threads, pockets, or tight bends where product or coolant can stagnate.
  • Polished surface finish. A 32Ra (or finer, to 20Ra/15Ra) interior minimizes the microscopic peaks and valleys that harbor bacteria.
  • Corrosion-resistant stainless. 304 or 316L stainless is antimicrobial, easy to clean, and stands up to CIP/SIP cycles.
  • Cleanable in place. Smooth, fully drainable geometry lets the system be flushed without being taken apart.

Connection types explained

Sanitary fittings connect in a few standard ways. Tri-clamp (tri-clover) joints use two ferrules, a gasket, and a clamp for fast, tool-free disassembly — ideal where lines are opened for cleaning or reconfiguration. Butt weld joints are welded permanently for the smoothest, most leak-proof run. Bevel-seat and I-Line threaded unions give a strong mechanical hold for higher-vibration service. Most real systems combine welded runs with clamped connections at points that need service.

Sanitary fittings for data center liquid cooling

As AI and high-density computing push rack loads past 30–100 kW, data centers are adopting the same sanitary stainless construction proven in food and pharma. Welded and clamped 316L fittings carry deionized water and glycol coolant through direct-to-chip and immersion loops with no leach path and no crevice to trap contaminants — critical when fluid runs inches from live hardware. Cardinal supplies the full fitting set alongside sanitary tubing and valves to build a complete loop. See our data center cooling solutions.

clamp-ferrules.seo_content:
Sanitary Clamp Ferrules

A clamp ferrule is the flanged end that turns a plain tube into a serviceable, leak-tight connection. Welded to the tube, two ferrules meet with a gasket between them and a tri-clamp around the outside to form a hygienic clamp joint — the tool-free, openable connection at the heart of every sanitary system. Cardinal Cooling Systems stocks sanitary clamp ferrules in 304 and 316L, 3-A certified with a 32Ra finish, from ½" to 12".

Also called a tri-clamp ferrule or weld ferrule, it is the most common way to terminate sanitary tube for a clamp connection. Because the joint disassembles in seconds without tools, clamp ferrules make lines easy to clean, inspect, and reconfigure — which is why they're standard in data center liquid cooling, food and beverage, dairy, and pharmaceutical systems.

How a tri-clamp joint works

A complete sanitary clamp connection uses three parts: two ferrules (one welded to each tube end), a gasket seated between their faces, and a clamp that pulls the two flanges together. Tighten the clamp and the gasket compresses into a leak-tight, crevice-free seal; loosen it and the line opens for cleaning. The ferrule provides the machined flange face that makes that seal possible.

Types of clamp ferrules we stock

  • Long weld ferrule — extra body length for easier welding and alignment; the most versatile everyday ferrule
  • Short weld ferrule — a compact body for tight spaces where welding room is limited
  • Heavy wall / tank weld ferrule — thicker wall and longer body for welding into tanks and vessels or higher-pressure service
  • Reducing ferrule — steps between two tube sizes at the clamp connection
  • Automatic (orbital) weld ferrule — long tangents made for orbital welding equipment and high-purity work
  • Roll-on ferrule — slides over existing tube before welding (note: not a 3-A seamless joint)

Long weld vs. short weld — quick answer

Choose a long weld ferrule when you have room and want the easiest, best-aligned weld — it's the default for most installs. Choose a short weld ferrule when space behind the flange is tight. Both share the identical tri-clamp flange, so either mates to the same gaskets and clamps; the only difference is how much tube length you have to weld.

Clamp ferrules for data center liquid cooling

Liquid-cooling loops need points that open for service without cutting pipe. Welding 316L clamp ferrules onto the sanitary tubing at CDUs, manifolds, filters, and pumps creates tri-clamp joints that let technicians break the loop, swap components, and reconnect in minutes — with a gasket-sealed, crevice-free connection that resists glycol and deionized water. hex-nuts.seo_content:
Sanitary Hex Nuts

A sanitary union hex nut is the hexagon-shaped, threaded nut that draws a bevel seat union together — the part that tensions a threaded bevel ferrule against a plain bevel ferrule to form a rigid, leak-tight joint. Cardinal Cooling Systems stocks sanitary hex nuts in 304 stainless steel, from 1" to 4", built to the Acme thread standard used across the sanitary fittings industry.

Also called a hex head nut or bevel seat hex nut, this hexagon nut is a distinct sanitary process component — not a general mechanical fastener — purpose-built for the bevel seat (Acme thread) union style still common in dairy, food, and beverage lines. Its coarse, trapezoidal Acme thread and hex wrenching flats let a line be assembled and broken down by hand or wrench, without special tools.

How a bevel seat union works

A complete bevel seat union has three parts: a threaded bevel ferrule and a plain bevel ferrule (each welded to a tube end), and the hex union nut that threads over both and draws their beveled faces together. As the nut tightens, the two bevel faces seat against each other in a rigid, metal-to-metal contact — no gasket required for a positive seal, though one can be added on request for extra sealing margin.

Why the Acme thread — and why it's self-sealing

  • Contamination-tolerant. Acme's coarse, trapezoidal profile is far less prone to jamming or galling than fine machine threads if a little product or debris gets into the joint — important in a process environment.
  • Even load distribution. The trapezoidal thread spreads clamping force evenly around the joint, helping the bevel faces seat consistently.
  • Self-sealing by design. The bevel-to-bevel metal contact seals the union on its own. This is what makes these self-sealing hex nuts — the seal comes from geometry and clamping force, not a gasket.
  • Fast hand assembly. The hex flats let the nut be run down and tightened without specialty tools, and the union breaks down just as quickly for cleaning or reconfiguration.

Bevel seat vs. tri-clamp

A bevel seat union uses this threaded hex nut for a rigid, self-sealing metal-to-metal joint and is common in legacy and modern dairy, food, and beverage lines that were built to that standard. A tri-clamp connection instead uses a gasket between two ferrules held by an external clamp, and is the more common modern standard for fast, tool-free disassembly. If you're matching or replacing parts on an existing bevel seat line, stay with the hex nut union; for new builds, tri-clamp is typically the default.

bevel-seat-gaskets.seo_content:
Bevel Seat Gaskets

A bevel seat gasket is the small part that makes the whole tri-clamp joint work — a flat sealing ring compressed between two ferrule faces to form a leak-tight, sanitary connection. Cardinal Cooling Systems stocks standard bevel seat gaskets in EPDM, PTFE, Viton, and silicone, sized ½" to 12", for use on tri-clamp and other bevel seat fittings.

Picking the right seat gasket is a material decision as much as a size decision: the wrong compound can swell, harden, or fail against the fluid it's meant to seal. The right one seals reliably for years. Below is a straight guide to picking the right material for coolant, water, steam, or process fluid.

Gasket material selection guide

MaterialBest forNotes
EPDMWater, glycol, steam, general sanitary serviceEconomical default. Good with oils/fats, ozone, chemicals. NOT for mineral oils, solvents, or aromatic hydrocarbons. Rated roughly –30°F to 300°F.
PTFE (Teflon)Aggressive chemicals, water, steam, high-purityExcellent chemical resistance, very low extractables. More rigid — less forgiving of large temperature swings; use a high-pressure clamp for continuous service.
Viton (FKM)Oils, fuels, higher-temperature serviceStrong resistance to oils and heat; a common choice where EPDM is not chemically compatible.
SiliconeFood-contact, wide temperature rangeFlexible across a broad temperature band; platinum-cure grades used in food and pharma.
Envelope (PTFE/EPDM or PTFE/Viton)Aggressive media needing flexibilityPTFE outer shell over an EPDM or Viton core — combines chemical inertness with elastomer flexibility and sealing memory.

How to select the right gasket thickness for tri-clamp fittings

Standard tri-clamp gaskets are typically ⅛" (0.125") thick and match every standard ferrule size from ½" to 12". Some flanged/ANSI-pattern sanitary gaskets are also available in 1/16". Use the thickness specified for your ferrule and clamp style — mixing an unusual thickness into a standard joint is the most common cause of a gasket that won't seat evenly. Whatever the thickness, avoid overtightening the clamp: it compresses the gasket beyond its design range and can cause warping and leaks rather than a better seal.

Coolant & chemical compatibility

For data center liquid cooling loops carrying glycol mixes or deionized water, EPDM is the standard choice — it handles both fluids well and is economical for the number of joints in a typical loop. Where a dielectric fluid or oil-based coolant is used, EPDM is not compatible and Viton is the right substitute. For the highest-purity make-up water systems, PTFE or an envelope gasket minimizes extractables into the loop. If you're unsure which compound suits your coolant, request a quote and we'll confirm compatibility.

Gaskets for data center liquid cooling

Every tri-clamp joint in a cooling loop — at clamp ferrules, valves, adapters, and end caps — relies on the gasket, not the fittings, to actually seal. Choosing the correct compound for glycol or deionized-water service prevents the slow degradation that leads to weeping joints near live hardware. See our data center cooling solutions for the full loop.

sanitary-butt-weld-fittings.seo_content:
Sanitary Butt Weld Fittings

Sanitary butt weld fittings join stainless tube end-to-end into one smooth, crevice-free flow path — the permanent connection method specified wherever a line must stay leak-tight, fully drainable, and clean-in-place. Cardinal Cooling Systems stocks a complete range of stainless steel butt weld fittings in 304 and 316L, from ½" up to 12", each 3-A certified with a 32Ra polished interior and backed by mill test reports for full material traceability.

Because a welded joint has no gasket, thread, or clamp to trap fluid or harbor bacteria, buttweld fittings are the backbone of permanent hygienic and high-purity piping. They are the connection of choice in data center liquid cooling loops, breweries, dairies, and pharmaceutical process lines — anywhere a clean, low-turbulence, maintenance-free run matters more than the ability to disassemble.

Why engineers specify butt weld over clamp or threaded connections

  • Zero leak paths. A full-penetration weld becomes part of the tube — no gasket to fail, no thread to weep under thermal cycling or vibration.
  • Fully drainable, CIP-ready. The smooth interior bore lets systems be cleaned in place without dead legs where product or coolant can stagnate.
  • Lowest pressure drop. A flush, matched-ID joint keeps turbulence and head loss to a minimum across long supply and return runs.
  • Permanent and vibration-proof. Ideal for buried, embedded, or hard-to-access runs that will never need to be taken apart.

Butt weld vs. clamp vs. threaded — quick answer

Choose tri-clamp fittings where you need to disassemble for service or reconfiguration. Choose threaded/NPT adapters only to interface with instruments or existing pipe. Built for data center liquid cooling

As rack densities push past 30–100 kW, direct-to-chip and immersion cooling loops rely on the same sanitary stainless construction long trusted in food and pharma. Welded 316L headers carry deionized water and glycol coolant with no leach path and no gasket to degrade — critical when a single drop near live hardware is a facility event. Sanitary Adapters

A tri-clamp adapter is the bridge between a hygienic clamp system and everything that isn't — threaded pumps, instruments, hoses, and existing pipe. Every adapter for pipe in this category has a sanitary clamp end on one side and a different connection standard on the other — letting a clean, cleanable process or cooling loop interface with the threaded equipment it inevitably has to meet somewhere. Choosing the right tube fitting adapter is about matching two things correctly: the thread standard and the thread gender.

Adapter types we stock

  • Tri-clamp × male NPT — threads into a female NPT port; self-sealing tapered thread
  • Tri-clamp × female NPT — accepts a male NPT pipe or fitting
  • Tri-clamp × BSP (BSPT/BSPP) — for equipment built to British Standard Pipe thread
  • Tri-clamp × hose barb — connects to EPDM, PTFE, or silicone hose for flexible runs
  • Tri-clamp × camlock — quick-connect/disconnect for temporary or transfer connections
  • Tri-clamp × flange — interfaces with ANSI, DIN, or JIS flanged equipment

NPT vs. BSP — quick answer

NPT (National Pipe Thread) is the tapered US standard; it self-seals as the tapered threads wedge together, typically without tape or sealant. BSP (British Standard Pipe) is common outside the US and comes in two forms: BSPT (tapered, self-sealing like NPT) and BSPP (parallel, which needs a gasket or O-ring to seal since the straight threads alone won't). NPT and BSP look similar but are not interchangeable — mixing them causes leaks or damaged threads. Always match the adapter's thread standard to your existing equipment.

Why threaded adapters aren't 3-A certified

Any connection with exposed threads cannot carry 3-A sanitary certification, because thread roots can't be fully cleaned in place. That's expected and fine: an adapter's job is to be the one transition point where a system meets threaded equipment, while the clamp side keeps the rest of the run fully sanitary. Keep threaded connections to the minimum needed and use tri-clamp for everything else.

Adapters for data center liquid cooling

Cooling distribution units, pumps, and existing chilled-water infrastructure often present NPT or BSP threaded ports, while the sanitary loop around them runs tri-clamp. Adapters make that connection clean: a 316L tri-clamp-to-NPT or tri-clamp-to-BSP adapter lets the loop tie into a CDU inlet or an existing threaded header without compromising the hygienic, leak-resistant construction of the rest of the run. Sanitary Valves

Sanitary valves control the flow of fluid through a hygienic system — starting, stopping, throttling, or diverting it — without the crevices, threads, or dead spots where bacteria could grow. Cardinal Cooling Systems is a US supplier of sanitary valves in 304 and 316L stainless steel — ball, butterfly, and check valves — with polished 32Ra wetted surfaces, tri-clamp or weld ends, and manual or actuated operation.

A sanitary valve differs from an industrial one in the details that make it cleanable: mirror-polished contact surfaces, inert seats and seals (EPDM, Viton, silicone, or PTFE), and hygienic connections instead of threads. That construction lets the whole line be cleaned in place (CIP) or sterilized in place (SIP), which is why sanitary valves and fittings are standard in data center liquid cooling, food, beverage, dairy, and pharmaceutical processing.

  • Check valves — automatic, passive backflow prevention to protect pumps and upstream equipment.

How to choose the right sanitary valve

  • For tight on/off shutoff: choose a ball valve — a full-bore path, minimal pressure drop, and reliable sealing for frequent cycling in smaller lines.
  • For compact, economical isolation and throttling: choose a butterfly valve — light, short in the line, and cost-effective in larger sizes such as 3"–12" headers.
  • For backflow prevention: choose a check valve — passive, one-way protection for pumps and process equipment with no actuation required.

As rack densities climb past 30–100 kW, liquid cooling loops need reliable, cleanable flow control. Butterfly valves isolate and balance large chilled-water and coolant headers economically; ball valves give tight shutoff at branches and CDU connections; and check valves protect pumps from backflow. In 316L with EPDM seats, these valves handle glycol and deionized water without seat degradation or leaching. Pair them with sanitary tubing, butt weld fittings, and clamp ferrules to build the loop, or see our data center cooling solutions.

Their light weight and low cost in larger line sizes make them the go-to choice for isolating and balancing main supply and return runs.

Why choose a butterfly valve

  • Compact, space-saving. A wafer-style body adds almost no length to the line — ideal for tight rack rows and crowded skids.
  • Economical at larger sizes. Cost advantage over ball valves grows as line size increases, making them efficient for 3"–12" headers.
  • Low flow resistance, bi-directional. The large open disc area gives minimal pressure drop and gentle, reversible flow.
  • Easy to install and service. On clamp systems the valve drops straight into an existing tri-clamp joint — no gaskets or welding, just the clamp. Seats are field-replaceable.

Configurations we stock

  • Manual clamp butterfly valves — multi-position locking handle for set-and-hold throttling or isolation
  • Pneumatic (air-actuated) butterfly valves — including spring-return, fail-safe (normally closed) for automated loops
  • Electric-actuated butterfly valves — for remote or signal-driven control
  • Weld-end and tri-clamp end connections — match your line's connection method
  • Seat options: EPDM, Viton, and silicone — chosen to suit the coolant or process fluid

Butterfly valve vs. ball valve — quick answer

Choose a butterfly valve for compact, economical isolation and throttling of clean, low-to-medium-viscosity fluids, especially in larger line sizes. Choose a sanitary ball valve when you need a full unobstructed bore, the tightest shutoff, or frequent on/off cycling in smaller lines. Many cooling and process systems use butterfly valves on the large headers and ball valves at the branches — both are part of our full sanitary valves range.

Built for data center liquid cooling

In direct-to-chip and immersion cooling systems, butterfly valves isolate and balance the primary chilled-water and secondary coolant loops where compactness and cost matter most. A 316L disc and body with an EPDM seat stands up to glycol mixes and deionized water without leaching or seat degradation, and the quarter-turn action makes fast isolation simple during service. Seat material selection

EPDM is the default for water, glycol, and deionized-water cooling loops and handles temperatures to roughly 250°F. Choose Viton for oils, fuels, and aggressive chemicals, and silicone for high-purity or wide-temperature applications. Avoid Buna/nitrile in deionized-water service. Sanitary Tubing

Sanitary tubing is the backbone of every hygienic and liquid-cooling line — polished stainless steel tube built to carry fluid cleanly, with a smooth interior and no crevices where residue or bacteria could collect. Cardinal Cooling Systems is a US stainless steel sanitary tubing supplier stocking 304 and 316L tube manufactured to ASTM A270 and 3-A standards, polished to a 32Ra finish, and available cut to size with full material traceability.

Unlike ordinary pipe, stainless steel sanitary tube is specified by exact outside diameter (OD) and wall thickness and finished to a controlled surface roughness, so it welds cleanly to fittings and cleans in place. That precision is why sanitary stainless steel tubing is standard in data center liquid cooling, food, beverage, dairy, and pharmaceutical systems.

Surface finish explained

  • 32Ra (standard). A 32-microinch roughness average — the baseline sanitary finish that resists bacterial attachment and cleans in place. Standard on tube OD.
  • 20Ra ID. A smoother interior polish for higher-purity service; standard on many A270 tubes and required by many food and dairy specs.
  • 15Ra / electropolished. Mirror finish for pharmaceutical and biopharma (ASME BPE) lines where biofilm prevention is critical.

304 vs. 316L tubing

304 is the economical workhorse for general sanitary and water service. 316L adds molybdenum for markedly better resistance to chlorides, glycol, and deionized water and, with its lower carbon content, welds more cleanly — the reason it is the default for cooling loops and high-purity lines. For any deionized-water cooling or pharmaceutical application, specify 316L. See our full guidance on 304 vs 316 stainless.

Sanitary tubing for data center liquid cooling

In direct-to-chip and immersion cooling, tubing forms the supply and return headers that carry coolant to CDUs and rack manifolds. Polished 316L tube resists the deionized water and glycol used in these loops without leaching or pitting, and its smooth bore keeps pressure drop and turbulence low across long runs — critical as rack densities climb past 30–100 kW.
